The crossover point occurs when post-hoc rejection exceeds $\sim$70\%: Mistral DocRED rejects 73.7\% of predicted triples, discarding enough true positives that constrained decoding's recall advantage dominates ($+$1.67\,pp).
OntoCoDec's advantage thus scales with violation severity: precisely when constraints are most needed, post-hoc filtering is most destructive.
Under fine-tuning, both strategies converge because few violations remain to filter or constrain ($\Delta \leq 0.55$\,pp across all four FT groups, with each strategy winning two).

%%% Zero-Shot Runtime Profiling %%%

\paragraph{Zero-Shot Runtime Profiling.}
\label{app:runtime}

On SciERC (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot greedy, NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition), unconstrained inference averages 4.163\,s/doc and Full S1 constrained decoding averages 4.710\,s/doc ($+$13.1\% overhead).
On DocRED (same configuration), unconstrained inference averages 19.34\,s/doc and Full S1 averages 19.81\,s/doc ($+$2.43\% overhead).
The lower relative overhead on DocRED reflects amortization: the fixed per-token constraint cost is spread over longer generation sequences.
Grammar compile is a one-time 0.044\,s cost (amortized to zero).

% exp_id: p8c_ft_scierc_latency — Reviewer Report #23 verified
\paragraph{Fine-Tuned Latency Profiling.}
\label{app:ft-latency}
Under LoRA fine-tuning (same hardware and dataset), unconstrained inference averages 2.612\,s/doc and Full S1 constrained decoding averages 2.873\,s/doc ($+$10.0\% overhead, $n{=}551$).
Fine-tuned models generate shorter, more structured outputs than zero-shot models (2.612\,s vs.\ 4.163\,s/doc unconstrained), reducing absolute generation time by 37\%.
The relative overhead ($+$10.0\%) is slightly lower than zero-shot ($+$13.1\%), consistent with shorter sequences requiring fewer constraint checks per document.

%%% Fuzzy Relation Matching %%%

\paragraph{Relation Matching Protocol.}
\label{app:fuzzy-matching}
Relation F1 evaluation uses fuzzy normalization to handle model-specific formatting variants (e.g., underscores vs.\ spaces, abbreviations).
A predicted relation $r_p$ matches gold relation $r_g$ if: (1)~exact string match after case-insensitive normalization, or (2)~token overlap $>$80\% \emph{and} edit distance $\leq 2$.
This protocol affects primarily Mistral, which produces underscore-separated variants (e.g., ``head\_of\_government'' for ``head of government'').
On Mistral DocRED, fuzzy matching contributes 98 additional TPs ($+$0.84\,pp R-F1; strict R-F1\,=\,3.50\% vs.\ fuzzy 4.34\%).
For Qwen and Llama under grammar constraints, the grammar layer enforces exact relation names, making fuzzy matching irrelevant (0 additional matches).
All F1 figures in the main text use fuzzy normalization consistently across all models and conditions.

%%% WikiEvents Extended %%%

\paragraph{WikiEvents Dataset Details.}
\label{app:wikievents}
WikiEvents~\cite{li2021document} is a document-level event argument extraction benchmark grounded in the DARPA KAIROS ontology.
It defines 56 event types, 80 argument roles, and 27 entity types, with 245 (event\_type, role)$\to$allowed\_entity\_types constraints.
The grammar layer targets EV (event vocabulary), RoV (role vocabulary), and ET; the semantic layer enforces AC (argument constraint) via role-conditioned masking, analogous to RE domain/range enforcement.

1	\section{Reproducibility Details}
2	\label{app:reproducibility}
3	
4	\paragraph{Fine-tuning configuration.}
5	All four fine-tuned models (Qwen3-8B and Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct on SciERC and DocRED) use identical LoRA hyperparameters: rank $r{=}16$, $\alpha{=}32$, dropout $0.05$, no bias, targeting all attention and MLP projection layers (\texttt{q\_proj}, \texttt{k\_proj}, \texttt{v\_proj}, \texttt{o\_proj}, \texttt{gate\_proj}, \texttt{up\_proj}, \texttt{down\_proj}).
6	Training uses AdamW with learning rate $2{\times}10^{-4}$, cosine schedule, warmup ratio $0.1$, effective batch size $16$, bf16 precision, gradient checkpointing, and completion-only loss for 3 epochs.
7	SciERC trains on 1,762 examples (260 dev) for 333 steps; DocRED trains on 3,053 examples (998 dev) for 573 steps.
8	Maximum sequence length is 2,048 (SciERC) and 4,096 (DocRED).
9	All runs use seed 42.
10	
11	\paragraph{Hardware and software.}
12	Training runs on a single NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU (98\,GB VRAM).
13	SciERC fine-tuning takes approximately 11 minutes per model; DocRED takes approximately 1.5 hours.
14	Software versions: PyTorch 2.10, Transformers 4.57, PEFT 0.19, TRL 1.1, Accelerate 1.13.
15	
16	\paragraph{Inference time.}
17	Inference timing is reported in Appendix~\ref{app:runtime} (NVIDIA RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Server Edition GPU, same hardware as training).
18	Full S1 constrained decoding adds $+$13.1\% wall-clock overhead on SciERC and $+$2.43\% on DocRED (Qwen3-8B, zero-shot greedy); under LoRA fine-tuning, overhead is $+$10.0\% on SciERC.
19

1	\section{Ontology Scalability}
2	\label{app:scalability}
3	
4	\begin{table}[h]
5	\centering
6	\small
7	\resizebox{\columnwidth}{!}{%
8	\begin{tabular}{@{}lrrrr@{}}
9	\toprule
10	\textbf{Scale} & \textbf{Types} & \textbf{Rels} & \textbf{Compile (s)} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
11	\midrule
12	Small (SciERC) & 6 & 7 & 0.33 & 1.02$\times$ \\
13	Medium (DocRED) & 6 & 96 & 0.32 & 1.03$\times$ \\
14	Large (synth.) & 100 & 500 & 0.35 & 1.03$\times$ \\
15	XLarge (synth.) & 200 & 1{,}000 & 0.42 & 1.03$\times$ \\
16	\bottomrule
17	\end{tabular}}
18	\caption{Compilation time (one-time) and per-token inference overhead across ontology scales. Small and Medium use real ontologies; Large and XLarge use synthetic ontologies with random domain/range constraints. Overhead measured on Qwen3-8B, 10 documents per scale.}
19	\label{tab:scalability}
20	\end{table}
21	
22	Grammar compilation scales sub-linearly (0.33\,s to 0.37\,s for 7$\to$1{,}000 relations); semantic constraint compilation grows linearly but remains negligible (0.4\,ms to 17\,ms).
23	Inference overhead is constant at 2--3\% because XGrammar uses precompiled bitmasks ($O(1)$ per token) and the semantic layer checks only the active relation's domain/range set rather than the full ontology.
24	The practical limit is first-token uniqueness: when entity types exceed $\sim$200, prefix collisions in the tokenizer vocabulary may require fallback to multi-token disambiguation (\S\ref{sec:dynamic-masking}).
25

1	\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
2	\label{app:beam-search}
3	
4	OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
5	The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
6	Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.
7	
8	\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
9	Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
10	(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
11	Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
12	(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
13	Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
14	Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.
15	
16	\paragraph{Results.}
17	Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.
18	
19	\begin{table}[h]
20	\centering
21	\small
22	\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
23	SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
24	ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
25	\label{tab:beam-search}
26	\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
27	\toprule
28	\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
29	\midrule
30	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
31	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
32	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
33	\midrule
34	\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
35	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
36	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
37	\midrule
38	\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
39	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
40	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
41	\midrule
42	\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
43	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
44	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
45	\midrule
46	\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
47	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
48	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
49	\midrule
50	\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
51	  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
52	  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
53	\bottomrule
54	\end{tabular}
55	\end{table}
56	
57	\paragraph{Discussion.}
58	For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
59	On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
60	On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
61	Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
62	The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.
63	
64	Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
65	On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
66	On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
67	This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.
68	
69	\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
70	Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.
71	
72	\begin{table}[h]
73	\centering
74	\small
75	\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
76	\label{tab:beam-ablation}
77	\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
78	\toprule
79	$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
80	\midrule
81	1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
82	2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
83	4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
84	8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
85	\bottomrule
86	\end{tabular}
87	\end{table}
88	
89	DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
90	CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
91	$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.
92	
93	\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
94	Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
95	Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
96	Llama-3.1-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints and beam search ($k{=}4$) likewise achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) with R-F1=46.11; the zero-violation result thus generalizes across calibrated model families.
97	% exp_id: q1_llama_ft_beam_scierc
98	The three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are thus fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.
99	
100	Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
101	Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.
102	
103	\paragraph{Latency overhead.}
104	Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency} reports wall-clock latency for greedy and beam search ($k{=}4$) under LoRA fine-tuning.
105	
106	\begin{table}[h]
107	\centering
108	\small
109	\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
110	\toprule
111	\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{s/doc} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
112	\midrule
113	Greedy unconstrained   & 2.612 & 1.00$\times$ \\
114	Greedy constrained (S1)& 2.873 & 1.10$\times$ \\
115	Beam-4 unconstrained   & 3.446 & 1.32$\times$ \\
116	Beam-4 constrained (S1)& 4.013 & 1.54$\times$ \\
117	\bottomrule
118	\end{tabular}

\section{Beam Search Compatibility}
\label{app:beam-search}

OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is designed to be decoding-strategy agnostic.
The main experiments (\S\ref{sec:experiments}) use greedy decoding; Appendix~\ref{app:sampling} validates nucleus sampling.
Here we verify compatibility with beam search, completing coverage of the three standard decoding strategies.

\paragraph{Implementation challenges.}
Two stateful components require adaptation for beam search.
(1)~The grammar layer (XGrammar) maintains an internal \texttt{GrammarMatcher} state that tracks the generated token sequence; beam reordering invalidates this state because beams are permuted across steps.
Our solution instantiates a fresh \texttt{GrammarMatcher} per beam per step and replays the beam's current token sequence through XGrammar's stateless accept API (64 lines of code).
(2)~The semantic layer's \texttt{TypeConstraintProcessor} accumulates entity and relation registries that assume a single generation path.
Our solution isolates state per beam by calling \texttt{detect()} on the full partial output at each step, reconstructing all entity/relation state from scratch for each beam independently (61 lines of code).
Both adaptations add ${\sim}125$ lines total without modifying the existing greedy/sampling logic.

\paragraph{Results.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-search} compares beam search ($k{=}4$, \texttt{early\_stopping=True}) against greedy decoding under full S1 constraints across six model-dataset combinations.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Beam search ($k{=}4$) vs.\ greedy decoding under full S1 constraints.
SciERC evaluated on full test set (551 documents); DocRED evaluated on matched 50-document subsets (same documents for greedy and beam).
ET = entity type, RV = relation vocabulary, DR = domain/range, CF = cross-field consistency violation rates (\%); F1 $\times$ 100.}
\label{tab:beam-search}
\begin{tabular}{@{}llcccccc@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Model / Dataset} & \textbf{Decoding} & ET & RV & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.53} & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Qwen3-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 8.69 & 2.08 & 59.08 & 8.33 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.55} & 58.64 & 9.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 0.08 & 6.56 & 23.49 & 2.54 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.93} & 25.04 & 3.33 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Llama-3.1-8B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 1.58 & 6.85 & 55.35 & 6.12 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{0} & \textbf{0.94} & 55.62 & 9.47 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / SciERC (551)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 13.40 & 1.27 & 27.46 & 3.67 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & 13.79 & \textbf{0.57} & 26.66 & 4.37 \\
\midrule
\multirow{2}{*}{Mistral-7B / DocRED (50)}
  & Greedy      & 0 & 0 & 28.37 & 0.34 & 51.60 & 4.19 \\
  & Beam ($k{=}4$) & 0 & 0 & \textbf{21.37} & \textbf{0.19} & 51.78 & 5.70 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\paragraph{Discussion.}
For calibrated models (Qwen3-8B, Llama-3.1-8B), beam search achieves DR=0\% across all four model-dataset combinations (both SciERC with 7 entity types, 551 documents, and DocRED with 96 relation types, 50 documents), regardless of schema complexity.
On SciERC, beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (0.93\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (0.08\%\,$\to$\,0\%), and substantially reduces CF (Qwen: 9.90\%\,$\to$\,0.53\%; Llama: 6.56\%\,$\to$\,0.93\%).
On DocRED (matched 50-document subsets), beam search eliminates DR for both Qwen (8.69\%\,$\to$\,0\%) and Llama (1.58\%\,$\to$\,0\%), with CF reductions of 74\% and 86\% respectively.
Llama DocRED shows the largest R-F1 gain ($+$3.4\,pp), consistent with beam search recovering valid type assignments that greedy decoding missed due to constraint fallback.
The CF reduction is an indirect effect: beam search reduces constraint-fallback frequency by exploring alternative token sequences that satisfy both grammar and semantic masks simultaneously, avoiding the fallback-to-grammar path that produces cross-field inconsistencies under greedy decoding.

Mistral-7B-v0.3 constitutes a boundary condition on both datasets.
On SciERC (7 entity types), beam search does not reduce DR (13.4\%\,$\to$\,13.8\%), though CF drops by 55\% relative (1.27\%\,$\to$\,0.57\%) and R-F1 improves by $+$0.7\,pp; the unchanged DR confirms that all residual violations stem from entity type misclassification, not constraint-search failure.
On DocRED (96 relation types), beam search reduces DR by 25\% relative (28.4\%\,$\to$\,21.4\%): the more complex schema introduces constraint-search failures that beam exploration resolves, but the entity misclassification component remains.
This contrast reveals that beam search resolves constraint-search failure (where greedy decoding encounters $G(t) \cap S(t) = \emptyset$ conflicts) but cannot overcome fundamental model calibration limitations in entity typing.

\paragraph{Beam width ablation.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-ablation} varies beam width $k \in \{1,2,4,8\}$ on Qwen3-8B / SciERC (551 documents) under full S1 constraints.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\caption{Effect of beam width on constraint satisfaction and extraction quality (Qwen3-8B, SciERC, 551 documents, full S1 constraints). $k{=}1$ corresponds to greedy decoding.}
\label{tab:beam-ablation}
\begin{tabular}{@{}rcccc@{}}
\toprule
$k$ & DR$\,\downarrow$ & CF$\,\downarrow$ & E-F1$\,\uparrow$ & R-F1$\,\uparrow$ \\
\midrule
1 (greedy) & 0.93 & 9.90 & 30.98 & 8.36 \\
2          & 0.35 & 4.12 & 31.54 & \textbf{8.75} \\
4          & \textbf{0}    & 0.53 & 32.00 & 8.56 \\
8          & \textbf{0}    & \textbf{0.08} & \textbf{32.18} & 8.39 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

DR elimination at $k{\geq}4$ confirms that constraint-search failure is resolved with moderate exploration width.
CF continues to decrease with larger beam (0.08\% at $k{=}8$, only 2 residual violations), while entity extraction quality improves monotonically.
$k{=}4$ represents the optimal cost-effectiveness trade-off: it eliminates all DR violations at roughly half the compute cost of $k{=}8$.

\paragraph{Composability with fine-tuning.}
Under greedy decoding, the fine-tuned Qwen3-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints already achieves DR=0\% but retains CF=1.18\% (21 cross-field violations across 551 documents), with E-F1=67.05 and R-F1=43.77.
Adding beam search ($k{=}4$) eliminates all residual CF violations (1.18\%\,$\to$\,0\%), yielding zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) while preserving extraction quality (E-F1=66.88, R-F1=44.23; changes within $\pm$0.5\,pp).
Llama-3.1-8B (LoRA, SciERC) with full S1 constraints and beam search ($k{=}4$) likewise achieves zero violations across all four metrics (ET=0\%, RV=0\%, DR=0\%, CF=0\%) with R-F1=46.11; the zero-violation result thus generalizes across calibrated model families.
% exp_id: q1_llama_ft_beam_scierc
The three constraint mechanisms (grammar masking, semantic domain-range filtering, and beam exploration) are thus fully composable: each addresses a distinct violation source without interfering with the others or degrading task performance.

Beam search on DocRED introduces a modest increase in parse failures (3/50, 6\%) compared to greedy (1.1\%), as longer beam-generated sequences occasionally produce malformed JSON in complex documents.
Combined with the sampling robustness results (Appendix~\ref{app:sampling}), these findings confirm that OntoCoDec's constraint enforcement is compatible with greedy, sampling, and beam search decoding without modification to the core constraint logic.

\paragraph{Latency overhead.}
Table~\ref{tab:beam-latency} reports wall-clock latency for greedy and beam search ($k{=}4$) under LoRA fine-tuning.

\begin{table}[h]
\centering
\small
\begin{tabular}{@{}lrr@{}}
\toprule
\textbf{Condition} & \textbf{s/doc} & \textbf{Overhead} \\
\midrule
Greedy unconstrained   & 2.612 & 1.00$\times$ \\
Greedy constrained (S1)& 2.873 & 1.10$\times$ \\
Beam-4 unconstrained   & 3.446 & 1.32$\times$ \\
Beam-4 constrained (S1)& 4.013 & 1.54$\times$ \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\caption{Latency per document (SciERC, 551 docs, Qwen3-8B LoRA FT, RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell). Overhead relative to greedy unconstrained.}
\label{tab:beam-latency}
\end{table}

Beam search itself adds 32\% latency (4 beams); constraint overhead increases from 10\% (greedy) to 16.5\% (beam) because each beam independently maintains grammar and semantic state.
The total 1.54$\times$ overhead is acceptable for offline batch IE; \texttt{early\_stopping} limits additional compute to partial-sequence exploration.

We also explored a type-consensus constraint that forces identical entity types across all relations within a document.
However, CF violations occur precisely where the consensus type conflicts with domain-range constraints, creating a fundamental CF$\leftrightarrow$DR trade-off.
With DR-aware enforcement (skipping consensus when it would violate domain-range), the layer becomes a no-op (100\% skip rate on 551 SciERC documents and 50 DocRED documents).
This confirms that beam search resolves the CF$\leftrightarrow$DR tension through a fundamentally different mechanism: token-level exploration of paths satisfying both constraints simultaneously.
